Imported frozen strawberries from Egypt, said to be the cause of an outbreak of hepatitis A, have sickened 55 people in six states, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Wednesday 31 August\. CNN reports that health authorities confirmed 44 total infections in Virginia, where the outbreak first appeared, and additional infections in Maryland \(4\), West Virginia \(4\), North Carolina \(1\), Oregon \(1\) and Wisconsin \(1\)\.

About half of the 44 infected Virginians have been hospitalized, according to that state's department of health\. They range in age from 15 to 68\. Their symptoms began in early May through August, but health authorities did not develop the theory of a common source of infection until this month\.

The Virginia Department of Health originally connected the infection to smoothies, which contained the imported berries, served at Tropical Smoothie Café restaurants\.

Almost all those who became sick purchased smoothies at cafés in a limited region, including Virginia and neighboring states, reported the CDC\. The one sick person in Oregon had traveled to Virginia\.

\"On August 5, the Virginia Department of Health contacted us about a potential link between hepatitis A cases and frozen strawberries from Egypt,\" Mike Rotondo, CEO of Tropical Smoothie Café, said in a video posted August 21 on YouTube\. He added that the company immediately removed the imported strawberries from its cafes and purchased new strawberries from alternative sources\.

The Virginia Department of Health also announced its investigation of the outbreak on August 21\. The department said at the time that genetic tests showed the illnesses to be caused by a strain of hepatitis A virus associated with past outbreaks resulting from strawberries imported from Egypt\. On Friday, Virginia health authorities confirmed the link between the Egyptian fruit and local infections\.

Days after Storm Ida made landfall twice in Louisiana as a Category 4 hurricane, 2,000 volunteers from across the country have gone to the Gulf Coast to help the American Red Cross with recovery operations at \"ground zero,\" according to AccuWeather Prime presenter Adam Del Rosso\.

Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images

\"While no two catastrophes are similar,\" Joy Squier of the American Red Cross told Del Rosso, \"Ida undoubtedly left its imprint on Louisiana and up the coast\.\"

## Providing Shelter

Squier described Ida as a \"major tragedy,\" adding that the Red Cross is still trying to figure out where everyone in need is to get them into shelters with cool air, food, water, and other necessities\.

\"Every tragedy is unique, and this one was very severe,\" Squier said\.

## Red Cross Assistance

The Red Cross erected around 20 shelters across Louisiana, providing protection and other essentials to about 2,000 individuals\. Supplies that were given are also being distributed across the shelters and to other persons in need\.

In the aftermath of the hurricane, the Red Cross works with the government and community partners to determine the next steps for people who rely on shelters\.

According to Squier, people were still fleeing their houses and heading to shelters days after Ida made ashore\.

## Slowly Returning Home

Some individuals who fled ahead to the storm are beginning to return home, while others cannot return due to power outages and storm damage\. People in such situations can get health and mental health assistance from the Red Cross and a place to remain in one of the state's shelters and other basic requirements like food and water\.

## Hurricane Amidst the Pandemic

Getty Images

With the COVID-19 pandemic still a concern in the United States, Squier said additional considerations for volunteers, such as mask use, mandatory wherever inside Louisiana and COVID testing\.

\"COVID adds a difficulty,\" she explained, \"but it's nothing we can't handle\.\"

\"Time and time again, the people of Louisiana have been badly impacted,\" Squier added\. \"They're tenacious and proud\.\"

##  
Hurricane Ida

NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 29: Vehicles are damaged after the front of a building collapsed during Hurricane Ida on August 29, 2021 in New Orleans, Louisiana\. Ida made landfall earlier today southwest of New Orleans\. Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images

Hurricane Ida was the second-most destructive storm to hit the US state of Louisiana on record, after only Hurricane Katrina, and was tied for the strongest landfall in the state by maximum winds with Hurricane Laura a year earlier and 1856 Last Island hurricane\. Ida surpassed Ike in 2008 as the costliest storm on record\. The ninth named storm of the 2021 Atlantic hurricane season and the fourth hurricane and second significant hurricane\.

Ida formed as a tropical wave in the Caribbean Sea on August 26 and became a tropical depression\. The depression became stronger and became Tropical Storm Ida near Grand Cayman later that day\. Ida became a hurricane on August 27 due to favorable circumstances, right before passing across western Cuba\. The hurricane rapidly intensified over the Gulf of Mexico the next day, reaching its peak strength as a powerful Category 4 hurricane\.

#### **Tropic Air Belize Presents a New Livery**

Tropic Air has unveiled a modern new look to its iconic brand livery\. The new design which will be applied to all of the company’s aircraft was showcased today on a Cessna Caravan V3-HHW\.

Commenting on the new livery, John Greif III, President of Tropic said: “We’re a dynamic and innovative Belizean company\. We have so many exciting changes happening, that we thought the time had come for a new visual expression of who we are\. An expression that joins our past to our present, and sets the course for where we’re headed in the future\.”

“Despite challenging economic conditions, this is just one of many improvement projects that Tropic Air is investing in,” says Greif\. “We are investing in terminals, aircraft, infrastructure and staff every day…many of which the customer never notices\. In August, we will be opening a $10 million dollar state-of-the-art maintenance facility” he went on to say\.

Steve Schulte, the CEO, commented “We’ve tried hard to retain the essential elements of Tropic’s almost forty years of service and refine them for the future\. We’ve adapted the ‘tail fin’ to make it bolder and to reflect a simpler and more elegant shape…The job wasn’t to change who we are,” said Schulte, “We already know who we are\. The job was to keep the elements of Tropic that our employees and customers love, and to make them a bold, modern expression of our future\.”

The painting process has been simplified, using fewer maskings and less paint for a drastic reduction in materials used\. The new paint is also more durable so aircraft will require re-painting less often\. The iconic, Tropic logo, that appears on all aircraft, has been rejuvenated with a subtle makeover and detailing\.

Aircraft will receive the newly painted livery within the aircraft’s existing repainting schedule, and new aircraft delivered will also sport the new design\.

Press Release and picture courtesy of Tropic Air San Pedro, Ambergris Caye, Belize, July 30, 2015

# New SunJoya retail brand launches

Tierra Suelta has introduced SunJoya™, a new retail brand for premium tropical fruits, roots, vegetables and specialty products available throughout North America\.

\"An important differentiator is that we are actually growers as well as importers, and that was important to emphasize on the packaging for SunJoya,\" said Adrian Abreu, CEO of Tierra Suelta\. \"Our family has spent three generations honing the expertise it takes to grow exceptional tropical produce, but retailers need more than great fruit\. They need a partner who can make the supply chain easier to manage and the category more profitable\.\"

© Tierra Suelta*SunJoya is a new retail brand for premium tropical fruits, roots, vegetables and specialty products\.*

SunJoya gives the company's full portfolio a distinctive consumer-facing identity, including four varieties of Dragon Fruit, Florida-grown Mamey, Star Fruit, two varieties of Guava, tropical roots, and a wide selection of specialty items\.

Attractive packaging, approachable product information, and merchandising support help retailers engage the already loyal tropicals consumers while encouraging discovery among shoppers new to tropicals\.

\"SunJoya is more than a label\. It's a retail program built around consistency, flexibility and discovery,\" said Kristyn Lawson, retail sales specialist for Tierra Suelta\. \"It helps retailers introduce shoppers to exciting tropical flavors\. We also remain committed to giving buyers private label and custom packing options, plus hands-on support behind the scenes\.\"

According to Circana retail data reported by IFPA, U\.S\. tropical and specialty fruit sales grew 4\.5 percent year over year in August 2025, with dragon fruit and other specialty items continuing to gain momentum\.

© Tierra Suelta  
*L-R: Adrian Abreu, Kristyn Lawson, Karen Nardozza *

\"Tropical produce offers retailers tremendous opportunity, but the category can be complex,\" said Karen Nardozza, CEO and founder of Moxxy, the agriculture and fresh-food marketing agency that created the SunJoya brand\. \"We organized their broad product line to be inviting and easy to buy, connecting its supply-chain capabilities directly to less risk and shrink, stronger shopper engagement, and increased sales\.\"

Moxxy also created Tierra Suelta's new website, giving retailers quick access to its product portfolio and resources for building year-round tropical programs\.

A searchable catalog organizes 45 items into five categories: Dragon Fruit, Florida Grown, Roots & Vegetables, Tropical Fruit, and Specialty Tropicals\. Individual product pages provide flavor and texture profiles, shopper-relevant attributes, seasonality and a direct path to request pricing\.

\"The new site shows how our product breadth, combined with farming, packing, and logistics expertise, come together to deliver an elevated and dependable tropicals buying experience for retailers,\" said Abreu\.

# Tierra Suelta launches new website and SunJoya retail brand - FreshFruitPortal\.com

Tropical produce grower, packer, importer and shipper Tierra Suelta has launched a new website at tstropicals\.com, giving retailers quick access to its extensive product portfolio and resources for building dependable, year-round tropical programs\.

The launch also introduces SunJoya™, Tierra Suelta's new retail brand for premium tropical fruits, roots, vegetables and specialty products available throughout North America\.

## **A website built for produce buyers**

The vibrant, easy-to-navigate site was built around the questions produce buyers need answered quickly: What is available? When is it in season? How can it be packed? And what support is available to help it sell?

A searchable catalog organizes 45 items into five categories: Dragon Fruit, Florida Grown, Roots & Vegetables, Tropical Fruit, and Specialty Tropicals\. Individual product pages provide flavor and texture profiles, shopper-relevant attributes, seasonality, and a direct path to request pricing\.

### **Grower expertise sets Tierra Suelta apart**

\"An important differentiator is that we are actually growers as well as importers, and that was important to emphasize both on the new website and on the packaging for SunJoya,” said Adrian Abreu, CEO of Tierra Suelta\.

“Our family has spent three generations honing the expertise it takes to grow exceptional tropical produce, but retailers need more than great fruit\. They need a partner who can make the supply chain easier to manage and the category more profitable,\" Abreu said\.

\"The new site shows how our product breadth, combined with farming, packing, and logistics expertise, come together to deliver an elevated and dependable tropicals buying experience for retailers\.\"

### **More than a supplier, a retail partner**

A dedicated Retail Success section explains how Tierra Suelta supports year-round availability with custom packing, private label programs, merchandising assistance, and flexible delivery\. The company's in-house logistics team monitors shipments to distribution centers across the United States and Canada, helping maintain supply continuity and keep customers informed during weather, transportation, and market disruptions\.

Tierra Suelta's vertically integrated operations reinforce those retail benefits\. Produce is harvested and packed six days a week and quickly pre-cooled in temperature-controlled, Primus-certified facilities to protect flavor, extend shelf life and reduce shrink\. Full-time agronomists oversee production, and an in-house quality control team monitors each shipment\. Farms in Florida and Ecuador, supported by strategic sourcing partnerships across Latin America, provide promotable volume and reliable supply throughout the year\.

### **Tropical sales growth creates opportunity at retail**

According to Circana retail data reported by IFPA, U\.S\. tropical and specialty fruit sales grew 4\.5% year over year in August 2025, with dragon fruit and other specialty items continuing to gain momentum\.

\"Tropical produce offers retailers tremendous opportunity, but the category can be complex,\" said Karen Nardozza, CEO and Founder of Moxxy, the agriculture and fresh-food marketing agency that created the website and SunJoya brand\. \"We organized Tierra Suelta's broad product line to be inviting and easy to buy, connecting its supply-chain capabilities directly to less risk and shrink, stronger shopper engagement, and increased sales\.\"

### **SunJoya, private label, and custom packs provide more choice**

SunJoya gives Tierra Suelta's full portfolio a distinctive consumer-facing identity, including four varieties of Dragon Fruit, Florida-grown Mamey, Star Fruit, two varieties of Guava, tropical roots, and a wide selection of specialty items\.

Attractive packaging, approachable product information, and merchandising support help retailers engage the already-loyal tropicals consumers while encouraging discovery among shoppers new to tropicals\.

\"SunJoya is more than a label\. It’s a retail program built around consistency, flexibility and discovery,\" said Kristyn Lawson, retail sales specialist for Tierra Suelta\. \"It helps retailers introduce shoppers to exciting tropical flavors, but Tierra Suelta remains committed to giving buyers private label and custom packing options, plus hands-on support behind the scenes\.\"

# A new duo, Helado Tropical, makes experimental Latin pop with love and laughs - The World from PRX

Producer and singer-songwriterRoberto Carlos Lange creates experimental pop music as Helado Negro\. The son of Ecuadorian immigrants, he grew up in Florida in the ‘80s\.

Meanwhile, guitarist and songwriter Fabi Reyna was born in Mexico and makes indie-Latin-rock as Reyna Tropical\. Reyna, who uses they/them pronouns, grew up in Texas in the ‘90s\.

Then in 2024, the two were introduced to each other by a mutual friend and decided to write a song together\. Two years later, they became a band with a full album, both called “Helado Tropical\.”

Most of Helado Tropical’s songs — the lyrics in Spanish — are about emotions\. “Tocando,” or touching, is about someone longing for love\.

Most of Helado Tropical’s songs are about emotions and all the lyrics are in  
Spanish\.Gisele Regatão/The World

But the song’s music video is fun and silly\. The pair are in a grocery store wearing electric blue jumpsuits\. Mangoes fly around and Reyna sings while taking bites of a large papaya\.

The two shot the video at a Mexican supermarket in Portland, Oregon, where Reyna shops\. They explained the song shows the heart of Helado Tropical\. “Under the surface it’s really filled with running around, being at recess, jumping into the ocean,” Reyna said\. “‘Tocando’ is definitely the clearer indicator of this part of this relationship\.”

Even though Helado Negro is older — he’s 45 and Reyna is 34 — and has been in the music business longer, he said that that does not dictate what they create together\.

Dozens of fans attended Helado Tropical’s album release party at 360 Record Shop in Red Hook, Brooklyn, in July\.Gisele Regatão/The World

“The wisdom that I brought was: \[I\] don’t know anything, what is something new that can be made that has nothing to do with anything that I’ve done?” he said\. “That’s more interesting for me, that’s what I was looking forward to\.”

Reyna had another long music partnership before, but Nectali Diaz, the other half of that former duo — Reyna Tropical — died in an e-scooter accident in Los Angeles four years ago\.

It took a while after that loss for Reyna to be able to make music again, and they released the album “Malegría” solo in 2024\. Reyna said they are happy to collaborate with Helado Negro because the two have similar sensibilities\. “Our depth and our internal worlds are deep and ocean-like,” Reyna said\. “Put us together and it’s going to be very deep, sexy and playful too\.”

Helado Negro and Reyna Tropical were introduced by a mutual friend and became a band with a full album two years later called Helado Tropical\. Gisele Regatão/The World

They both wrote music and lyrics for the new album\. Helago Negro said “Dejate Caer” is one of his favorites\. “The song is a release for sure\. The words *Dejate Caer*, to let yourself fall, to let yourself go, to let loose, it’s such a special message,” he said\.

But these have been troubling times for the Latino community in the US, with the raids by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement \(ICE\) on migrant communities, that have led to killings, arrests and deportations\.

Reyna believes that makes their music more important than ever\. “What is the role of the artist?” they asked\. “In these times, it’s radical joy, it’s radical play, it’s radical pleasure, for us to remind our communities that we deserve this, we belong in this\.”

Sam Sumpter, an on-air host at WFUV, an eclectic music station in New York, interviewed Helado Tropical on her show, and said the two make a perfect match\.

Helado Tropical will tour the United States starting in San Diego in August\. They will be in New York City in October and then will wrap the tour in Mexico City in November\.Gisele Regatão/The World

“It was kind of a blind date in the music sense\. They got paired together and then just instantly hit it off, the chemistry was there,” she said\.

Sumpter, who is also the founder of the music blog Bands do Brooklyn, said their collaboration was possible because of the way music is often created today\.

“They’re both touring artists, they were out doing their thing and sending files back and forth and then meeting in random cities to fit in sessions where they can\. It’s cool that art can be made in this way now\.”

Helado Tropical’s music seems to resonate with fans of both musicians\. Nicole Motta, a photo art director who has been a fan of Reyna Tropical for years, was at an Helado Tropical’s concert at 360 Record Shop in Red Hook, Brooklyn, in mid-July\.

“I love them,” Motta said\. “They are doing experimental avant-garde in a way that is showing the reemergence of music from Indigenous and Latino cultures that I really enjoy\.”

Nicole Motta \(right\), a photo art director who has been a fan of Reyna Tropical \(left\) for years, was at an Helado Tropical’s concert in Red Hook, Brooklyn, in mid-July\.Gisele Regatão/The World

As Helado Tropical gets ready to tour dozens of cities starting in August, Helado Negro said he’s wondering what they will learn from each other\.

“Maybe too much, it’s going to be a lot of stories,” he said jokingly\. Reyna confessed they always turn to Helado Negro for advice\. “I’m always like, ‘Roberto, what should I do,’ so I’m worried more for him,” they said, laughing\.

Their first show is in San Diego on Aug\. 12 and they wrap the tour in Mexico City in November\.

# WEATHER VAULT: Hurricane Bob 1991

MEMPHIS, Tenn\. \(WMC\) -

Hurricanes in the Northeast are rare enough, but did you know the most recent hurricane landfall in the region was during an El Niño?

Between July and September of 1991, the Niño 3\.4 region was 0\.7 degrees Celsius, 1\.26 degrees Fahrenheit above average\.

At the same time, Hurricane Bob made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane on the coast of Rhode Island\.

The storm formed in the early hours of August 16, 1991 as a tropical depression before being named a tropical storm later that day\.

By August 17, 1991, Bob became a Category 1 hurricane off the east coast of Florida, but a cold front approaching the east coast quickly picked it up and accelerated it northwards\.

Bob strengthened into a Category 3 major hurricane off the coasts of North Carolina and Virginia on August 18, 1991\.

By the afternoon of August 19, 1991, Bob made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane on the coast of Rhode Island\.

Bob continued to track across New England, bringing a swath of damage through Rhode Island and Massachusetts before making another landfall as a tropical storm on the coast of Maine that evening\.

Even in slow and mostly inactive Hurricane seasons, memorable storms can still happen\. While the risk of getting hit is lower, it’s not zero\. It only takes one to make a name in the history books\.

# Forecasters watching two tropical systems

Created: Aug 12, 2026 08:43 PM \(Updated: Aug 12, 2026 09:02 PM\)

Tropical Storm Cristobal, well east of Bermuda and moving away as of 2\.45pm today \(Image from the Bermuda Weather Service\)

Tropical Storm Cristobal became the first named storm to form in the open Atlantic Ocean this year but does not appear to be a threat to Bermuda, the National Hurricane Centre reported\.

But forecasters are keeping an eye on a tropical wave located between the Lesser Antilles and Africa that as an 80 per cent chance of becoming a tropical depression\.

The Bermuda Weather Service said Cristobal was “well east” of Bermuda and heading away\.

As of 2\.45pm today, the storm was moving east at 25mph and carrying maximum winds of 45mph\.

The BWS said the tropical wave could become a tropical depression within two days\.

A tropical wave was halfway between the Lesser Antilles and Africa as of 2\.45pm today \(Image from the Bermuda Weather Service\)

A Facebook post from the BWS said: “Between an expected southerly track, strong wind shear and lots of dry air, \[the tropical wave\] does not look likely to be a threat to Bermuda, but we’ll keep an eye on it for sure\.

“Regardless it's a good time to remind everyone that as we head into the latter half of August, the tropics will become more active, so give those hurricane preparedness kits a check\.”

# How El Niño is neutralizing Atlantic hurricanes this season

PTIThis NOAA satellite image taken at 11:21 a\.m\. EST on Wednesday, Aug\. 12, 2026, shows Tropical Storm Cristobal in the Atlantic Ocean\.

The Atlantic hurricane season is showing signs of activity just as a powerful climate pattern threatens to keep tropical storms in check\.

Cristobal became the third named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season on Wednesday, but the system quickly weakened into a tropical depression over the open North Atlantic\. It is expected to dissipate by Thursday afternoon, according to CNN\.

The brief appearance of Cristobal comes as forecasters watch two other areas of disturbed weather in the Atlantic\. One has an 80% chance of developing into at least a tropical depression later this week, while another area farther east has a 50% chance of development\.

If another tropical storm forms, it will receive the name Dolly\.

## El Niño remains the biggest obstacle

The Atlantic may be approaching the period when hurricane activity normally begins to accelerate, but conditions are far from ideal for storms\.

The main problem is wind shear linked to El Niño\. Changes in wind speed and direction at different levels of the atmosphere can disrupt developing tropical systems, preventing them from organizing or causing existing storms to weaken\.

CNN reported that this hostile wind shear has become firmly established across parts of the Atlantic where tropical activity would normally be increasing\.

The situation could become even more challenging if El Niño strengthens into a potentially record-breaking Super El Niño later this year\.

## Atlantic hurricane season remains unusually quiet

The slow start has made 2026 one of the least active Atlantic hurricane seasons in years\.

Through August 11, only Arthur, Bertha and Cristobal had become named tropical storms\. CNN reported that this represents the quietest start to an Atlantic hurricane season since 2009\.

Arthur formed near the US Gulf Coast in June, while Bertha developed in late July\. Both systems encountered significant wind shear, limiting their ability to strengthen\.

Cristobal's development was notable for another reason: it was the first storm this season to form away from the immediate vicinity of the US coastline\.

The storm is not expected to threaten land and should weaken over colder waters in the North Atlantic\.

## New tropical threat faces a difficult path

The tropical Atlantic is now being closely watched for another potential system\.

The area with the highest chance of development is located in the Atlantic's main development region, where tropical systems typically become more numerous around this point in the season\. Warm ocean temperatures usually provide energy for storms, while weakening wind shear allows them to become better organized\.

This year, however, El Niño is disrupting that familiar pattern\.

Hurricane expert Phil Klotzbach of Colorado State University has described the wind shear as reaching record strength, according to CNN\. A brief improvement in conditions later this week could give the system enough time to organize into a tropical depression\.

But that opportunity may not last\. The system is expected to move west across the tropical Atlantic before encountering increasingly unfavorable wind shear near the eastern Caribbean\.

Another disturbance farther east also faces similar obstacles\.

## Hurricane season is behind its normal pace

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is noticeably lagging behind its typical timetable\.

A normal season generally produces at least three named storms by August 3 and four by August 15\. The first hurricane typically forms around August 11\.

That milestone has passed without a hurricane developing this year\.

There is still plenty of time for the Atlantic to become more active\. The busiest part of the season usually runs from mid-August through mid-October, meaning conditions could change quickly if wind shear weakens and ocean temperatures remain favorable\.

Still, the season's sluggish beginning has strengthened expectations that 2026 could remain relatively subdued\.

## NOAA raises odds of below-average season

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has become increasingly confident that the season will finish below average\.

NOAA's latest forecast update raised the probability of a below-normal hurricane season from 55% to 75%\. The agency also lowered its expected range for major hurricanes, cutting the outlook from one to three Category 3 or stronger storms to zero to two\.

Colorado State University has also projected a relatively muted season\.

If the Atlantic goes through the entire 2026 season without producing a major hurricane, it would mark the first such occurrence since 2013\.

For now, however, the tropics are entering the calendar period when activity typically picks up\. Whether the Atlantic finally wakes up or El Niño continues to suppress the season will depend heavily on whether the powerful wind shear begins to ease in the weeks ahead\.
